title: Sawdah, who made him smile
hookLine: a widow who joins his household after Khadijah, remembered for her humor and her open hand
carry: the one who made him smile

cards: A long night prayer. Bowing, and bowing, and still bowing.

Afterward, a woman of his household who prayed behind him comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and says: I prayed behind you last night, and you bowed so long I held my nose, in case it started to bleed.

And he laughs. That small joke is how Ibn Sa'd's book of early lives remembers her. She was a widow, the biographers say, who came into his household after Khadijah died, a house that had just lost its center.

teach.h: A WIDOW IN A GRIEVING HOUSE.
teach.b: Sawdah doesn't arrive in the story with a battle or a revelation attached to her name. She arrives in the ordinary rooms of a grieving home, and she brings lightness into them.
The reports about her are small, and that is the point of them. First, her humor.

teach.h: THE JOKE ABOUT THE LONG BOW.
teach.b: The joke about the long bow is a report in Ibn Sa'd, not in the two Sahih collections, so hold it as a story the early biographers kept.
It shows a person who could make the Prophet laugh about a long night of prayer, without making fun of the prayer. The laugh was at herself. Second, her generosity, and this one is in Bukhari.

teach.h: SHE GAVE HER DAY TO AISHA.
teach.b: When she grew older, Sawdah gave her turn, her day with the Prophet, to Aisha. Something she could have held on to, she handed to someone else, freely. Third, how the other wives saw her.

teach.h: I'D RATHER BE IN HER SKIN.
teach.b: In Sahih Muslim, Aisha says she never saw a woman she would rather be in the skin of than Sawdah, and adds, honestly, that Sawdah had a certain sharpness. A real person, then: quick, funny, a little fierce, and generous.
And one more scene from Bukhari. At the pilgrimage, Bukhari describes her as heavy and slow-moving, and she asked permission to leave Muzdalifah early, before the crowds. He gave it.
Aisha later wished she had asked too.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO MADE HIM SMILE.
teach.b: Put these together and Sawdah is remembered less for one great act than for the weather she made in a house: a laugh after a long night, a day handed over, an early start before the crowds.

how: Muslims count Sawdah bint Zam'ah among the mothers of the believers; the reports of her giving her day to Aisha and her early leaving at Muzdalifah come from Sahih al-Bukhari, and the stories of her humor from the early biographers.

games.q: the pilgrimage crowds will be crushing at dawn, and you move slowly. what do you do?
o: push through with everyone at dawn.
ask permission to leave Muzdalifah early, at night.
stay behind and skip the rest.
games.why: Bukhari says Sawdah asked to leave early, before the crowds, and the Prophet gave her permission; Aisha later wished she had asked too.

practice: Bring to mind someone in your life who is carrying something heavy right now, and look for something light you could offer them.
Sawdah's joke was at her own expense, so find one like that: a story on yourself, a silly moment from your week. If you pray, ask that your words lighten someone and wound no one.

wordCard.voice: Sawdah. A mother of the believers, remembered for making the Prophet laugh, and for giving her own day to Aisha. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: her name; she was Sawdah bint Zam'ah.

carryVoice: Your line: the one who made him smile. A small joke, kept by the biographers. See you tomorrow.
